chapter: Kansas City bands and the Blue Devils
title: Hiding odd notes in Basie's reed section; Ellington, Redman and Kenton
summary: Durham used organ harmony and flat fifths in Basie's reeds without writing accidentals; he compares Ellington, Redman and Kenton as creators who go out in space.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: But now they can hear anything, guys here -- augmented flats, 18 fifths and everything now. They know just what you're doing. And that was a little edge I had on them with the Basie band, (inaudible) was in the band. They say, we hear a peculiar sound in this reed section in that background. That's when I used to use organ harmony a lot, because you can dissolve odd sounds, and I'd always tell Earl, say, look make this a flat fifth. I'd say, but I don't want to put the accidentally in front of it, because -- like, you know how in this place, guys (inaudible) trying to see, what was that note I heard in there when he was holding that chord?
They'd look at it and do this, and everybody would laugh. You could tell --
But what it was, if it was a F flat,
F sharp, and it would be an F flat the way he'd make it, but I wouldn't let him put the signature there.
Yeah, they didn't know how to -- they'd say, oh, sure can bend those notes. So that's one of the tricks. I always did have an idea. I like to create.
And Duke, I don't know that much about him, but I know enough to know, he liked to create, and Don Redman.
So if you didn't hold him down with his own thing, he probably went on out in space because he wanted to hear something else.
Yeah, but he liked the (inaudible), too.

So you had to -- (inaudible) had to stop him to hold him back, was what we could do, because there wasn't no limit to where he could go. So that's Stan Kenton's idea, too. He'd keep on going if he could get by with it.
